title: Toward Associational Data Rights: A Digital Economy for Families & the Common Good | Institute for Family Studies
gist: A policy brief from an IFS-convened, ideologically cross-cutting working group (with RadicalxChange, OpenMined and University of Michigan Law) proposes a new legal framework of 'Associational Data Rights' — Data Rights Associations (DRAs) modeled on labor unions/farm co-ops that could force OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and other AI/data counterparties into mandatory collective bargaining over data use — arguing individual consent-based privacy law and top-down regimes like GDPR structurally fail because data value comes from aggregated, co-produced community information.

themes.theme: Measured Harm: AI and Family Formation

insights.claim: A 2026 NBER working paper estimates the iPhone's 2007 introduction may explain 33-52% of the decline in the general fertility rate among U.S. women aged 15-44 since the mid-2000s, attributed to displacement of in-person interaction and sexual intercourse by digital attention capture and pornography.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: One of the most concrete quantitative links yet cited between smartphone adoption and the fertility decline — relevant to any demographic/pro-natalist policy thesis and to how smartphone makers may be implicated in future family-welfare regulation.
insights.locator: The data-driven attention economy is also impeding family formation

insights.claim: AI 'companion' apps have grown 700% since 2022, and a 2026 Wheatley/IFS survey found 15% of dating, engaged, or married young adults regularly and covertly use romantic AI companions, with 34% having experimented with the behavior.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Quantifies a fast-growing AI-companion category with direct relevance to consumer-AI investment (e.g., Character.AI-style products) and to incoming family-policy scrutiny of the sector.
insights.locator: Since 2022, AI “companion” apps have increased by 700%

insights.claim: In that same survey, 54% of regular AI-romantic-companion users said they use the AI to replace real human relationships, 88% found the AI companion easier to open up to than their human partner, and 60% wished their real partner behaved more like their AI companion.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Suggests AI companion products are already substituting for, not supplementing, human partnerships at meaningful scale among couples — a durable demand driver for the category, but also a flashpoint for regulatory and religious-institution pushback.
insights.locator: 88% of regular dating or married romantic AI users reported finding AI companions easier to share feelings with

insights.claim: Regular engagement with a romantic AI companion was associated with a 46% lower likelihood of being in a stable relationship and a 40% decrease in the likelihood of quality communication with a spouse or partner.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The single most alarming causal statistic in the piece for the AI-companion sector: if replicated, it strengthens the case for age-gating, disclosure, or 'addictive design' litigation risk analogous to social-media lawsuits already targeting Meta and TikTok.
insights.locator: The study found that regular engagement with a romantic AI lowered the likelihood of being in a stable relationship by 46%

insights.claim: A 2026 JAMA Pediatrics study found 78% of parents and 69% of children use digital devices during family meals, and prior IFS/Wheatley (2023) research found 26% of respondents feared their marriage could end in divorce because of excessive tech use by a spouse.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Reinforces the 'device use degrades family cohesion' narrative that underpins demand for digital-wellbeing tools, parental-control products, and further platform regulation.
insights.locator: A 2026 study published in JAMA Pediatrics found that 78% of parents and 69% of children use digital devices during family meals

themes.theme: Core Thesis: Data as a Co-Produced Good

insights.claim: The report's central legal argument is that nearly all data fueling AI and the digital economy is 'co-produced' by users, their social contacts, and platforms together — not owned solely by whichever company happens to capture it — which should imply shared governance rights over its collection and use.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: This is the intellectual foundation for a proposed new legal category (associational data rights) that, if adopted, would materially raise compliance and data-licensing costs for every major AI/platform company; worth tracking as a legislative concept gaining institutional backing.
insights.locator: Part I argues that data is a co-produced good

insights.claim: Existing individual, consent-based privacy regimes fail structurally because a single user's data has limited value alone, but becomes highly valuable (and revealing about others) only in aggregate — meaning platforms can extract communal value while data subjects negotiate only individually and powerlessly.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Explains why GDPR/CCPA-style individual opt-outs haven't curbed platform data power — a mental model useful for evaluating whether any future privacy regulation (state or federal) will actually shift bargaining leverage away from Big Tech.
insights.locator: Individual data rights fail to rein-in asymmetric information power

insights.claim: Top-down technocratic privacy regimes like the EU's GDPR and Digital Services Act have had 'mixed success' and cannot keep pace with fast-evolving, opaque platforms, nor can they accommodate the differing values of pluralistic communities (e.g., religious groups vs. secular users) in a one-size-fits-all rule.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A direct critique of the EU regulatory model from a US policy-advocacy source — signals coming U.S. debate may explicitly reject the EU top-down approach in favor of a collective-bargaining model instead.
insights.locator: Top-down data privacy regimes are insufficient

insights.claim: Facebook's 2009-2012 experiment allowing users to vote on data-policy changes failed and was scrapped because ordinary users lacked the information and expertise to evaluate complex data terms, illustrating why democratic/individual approaches to platform governance don't scale.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A concrete historical precedent cited to argue that voluntary platform self-governance experiments reliably fail, which the report uses to justify mandatory (not voluntary) collective bargaining rights instead.
insights.locator: in 2009, Facebook responded to controversy over its abuse of user data

insights.claim: The report proposes three new legal rights — the Right of Digital Association, the Right to Collective Informational Bargaining, and the Right to Fair Representation — exercised through new entities called Data Rights Associations (DRAs), explicitly modeled on labor unions under the National Labor Relations Act.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: This is the report's core policy product: a union-like collective-bargaining structure for data/AI, which if enacted in any U.S. state or federally would create a wholly new regulatory counterparty for OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Amazon and TikTok to negotiate with.
insights.locator: Federal and state legislation should establish a new class of rights for the digital age

insights.claim: DRAs could compel 'covered' data counterparties into mandatory good-faith bargaining once membership thresholds are met (e.g., 25,000 affiliated data subjects, or $1,000,000 in annual revenue attributable to DRA-affiliated users), with a neutral arbitration panel resolving impasses via binding final-offer arbitration — modeled on the proposed Journalism Competition and Preservation Act (JCPA).
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete, low bar for triggering forced negotiation (25k users or $1M revenue) — a threshold companies of any AI/platform scale could hit quickly, making this a realistic near-term compliance/legal risk if adopted into law.
insights.locator: DRA-affiliated data subjects who collectively produce $1,000,000 in estimated annual revenue

insights.claim: Once a DRA is certified to bargain over one product, it can extend bargaining to 'substantially similar' products from the same or other companies — explicitly citing that a DRA certified for Google Search could also bargain over Gmail, Docs, and Maps, and a DRA certified for ChatGPT could also bargain with Anthropic over Claude's terms.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A cross-company bargaining-scope mechanism explicitly naming OpenAI/ChatGPT and Anthropic/Claude — flags a real (if speculative) future legal vector where one certified association could pressure multiple frontier AI labs simultaneously.
insights.quote: If a DRA were certified to bargain with OpenAI over ChatGPT’s terms, it could also bargain with Anthropic over Claude’s terms.
insights.locator: Scope of collective informational bargaining

insights.claim: The framework envisions DRAs funded via member fees, per-transaction cuts of data-counterparty payments, or ongoing equity-like revenue shares in the value generated by member data — rather than one-time payouts — giving them durable, recurring financial interest in data monetization outcomes.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: If implemented, this creates a new class of intermediary revenue claim on AI training-data monetization, comparable to how ASCAP/BMI extract ongoing royalties in music — a potential new cost line for AI labs licensing training data.
insights.locator: Financial sustainability

insights.claim: The proposal explicitly invites sector-specific DRAs — for authors negotiating AI-training compensation, gig workers preventing data extraction by platforms, faith-based organizations negotiating for 'moral virtue' aligned AI middleware, and free-speech DRAs negotiating anti-censorship terms with social platforms.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Signals where organized advocacy pressure on AI/data companies is likely to concentrate first if this model gains traction — creator/author compensation and gig-worker data rights look like the most legally mature analogues (cf. existing AI copyright suits).
insights.locator: Authors could also form DRAs to negotiate terms with tech companies

insights.claim: The authors ground DRAs in existing U.S. legal precedent for collective action overriding individual bargaining weakness: the Capper-Volstead Act of 1922 (farm cooperatives bargaining with grain buyers) and 1897 federal performance-rights law that spawned performing-rights organizations.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: These century-old precedents (agriculture antitrust exemption, music licensing collectives) are the closest legal analogues lawmakers would likely cite when evaluating whether a 'data union' concept is legally viable — useful for legal/regulatory risk modeling.
insights.locator: Precedent for the associational exercise of rights

insights.claim: The bargaining/arbitration mechanism explicitly mirrors the (unpassed) 2023 Journalism Competition and Preservation Act, which would have let news publishers jointly negotiate revenue-sharing with Big Tech platforms backstopped by binding arbitration.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Ties the DRA proposal to a specific piece of prior federal legislation that stalled — suggests DRA advocates will likely face similar political resistance (from tech lobbying) if reintroduced in a broader form.
insights.locator: The proposed Journalism Competition and Preservation Act of 2023 (JCPA)

themes.theme: Named Big Tech Practices and Vendors

insights.claim: OpenAI's Sam Altman is quoted describing his ideal AI as a 'super-competent colleague that knows absolutely everything about my whole life, every email, every conversation,' which the report frames as a vision that necessarily requires total surrender of personal data to AI companies to achieve.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Directly weaponizes an OpenAI executive's own stated product vision as evidence for the need for data-rights guardrails — indicates how AI-industry rhetoric about 'personal super-assistants' may become a regulatory liability.
insights.quote: a “super-competent colleague that knows absolutely everything about my whole life, every email, every conversation I’ve ever had, but doesn’t feel like an extension.”
insights.locator: Even when invasive data collection is inherent to a product

insights.claim: A cited 2024 Stanford report found some Big Tech companies retain users' chatbot conversations containing sensitive information for model training and may use it to target ads in other products, meaning ostensibly private AI chat disclosures can resurface as ad personalization elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A concrete privacy-leakage mechanism (chatbot conversation -> ad targeting) that is a plausible basis for future FTC action or class-action litigation against AI chatbot providers.
insights.locator: A 2024 report from Stanford researchers found

insights.claim: Identity-resolution firm LiveRamp is named as an example of a company that ties anonymized data to personally identifying information via 'identity graphs,' and Clearview AI is cited as enabling profiling/identification of bystanders captured in footage from devices like Meta's Ray-Ban smart glasses.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Names specific data-broker/surveillance vendors (LiveRamp, Clearview AI) as concrete regulatory targets under the proposed framework — relevant for assessing legal/reputational risk exposure of these companies and of Meta's smart-glasses hardware line.
insights.locator: The “ick factor” associated with videos captured by Ray-Bans

insights.claim: A 2026 Harvard Kennedy School report distinguishes 'external monetization' (selling/licensing data to other firms) from 'internal monetization' (using data in-house for targeting, product design, and engagement), identifying large vertically integrated firms like Meta and Google as especially reliant on the internal-monetization model.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A useful taxonomy for evaluating which companies (internal-monetizers like Meta/Google vs. external-monetizers/data brokers) are more exposed to different regulatory levers under any future data-rights regime.
insights.locator: A 2026 data economy report from Helena Malikova and the Harvard Kennedy School

insights.claim: The report invokes Cory Doctorow's 'enshitification' concept to describe how platforms diffuse data-production costs onto co-producing users while capturing an increasing share of the resulting value over time.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A widely-circulated critique framework (platform value-capture over time) applied here specifically to data monetization, citing Amazon's alleged use of vendor data to launch competing products as an example.
insights.locator: This dynamic, also termed “enshitification” by tech author Cory Doctorow

insights.claim: The report points to real, already-deployed technical building blocks that could make a DRA ecosystem feasible: a proposed 'Human Context Protocol' for portable user preferences, and the Global Privacy Control browser signal, which as of mid-2026 must be legally honored by covered businesses in 12 U.S. states.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Indicates state-level privacy infrastructure (opt-out signals) is already scaling (12 states by mid-2026) independent of any DRA legislation — a leading indicator of tightening compliance obligations for any consumer-data business.
insights.locator: As of mid-2026, 12 states require covered businesses to honor universal opt-out preference signals

insights.claim: Apple's Private Cloud Compute is cited as a working example of cryptographic attestation at consumer scale: before an iPhone sends user data to Apple's AI servers, each server must cryptographically prove it runs publicly inspectable software logged in a tamper-evident registry.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Apple is held up as the reference implementation for verifiable-compliance infrastructure that a future DRA-audit regime could piggyback on — relevant to Apple's positioning as the 'privacy-safe' AI vendor relative to competitors.
insights.locator: Apple's Private Cloud Compute already does this at consumer scale

insights.claim: Federated learning is already used at scale without centralizing raw data: Google has trained mobile-keyboard models via federated learning across hundreds of millions of phones since 2017, and ten pharmaceutical companies jointly trained drug-discovery models on 2.6 billion confidential data points without exposing each other's data.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Establishes that privacy-preserving multi-party computation is a mature, production-proven technology (Google since 2017; pharma industry consortium), lowering the technical-feasibility objection to any future collective data-governance/auditing regime.
insights.locator: Google has trained its mobile keyboard models leveraging FL across hundreds of millions of phones since 2017

insights.claim: The report proposes 'personhood credentials' to let DRAs verify authentic (non-bot) membership rolls without exposing personal information, addressing the risk that bad actors could inflate a DRA's bargaining power with fake or automated accounts.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Connects the data-rights proposal to the broader 'proof of human' verification trend already being built by AI/crypto identity projects — relevant to any thesis on personhood-verification infrastructure demand as AI-generated bot traffic grows.
insights.locator: Verified membership

themes.theme: A Cross-Ideological Coalition and Religious Framing

insights.claim: The report was produced by an explicitly cross-ideological 2025-2026 working group: Daniel Cochrane (IFS, family-conservative), Matt Prewitt (co-founder of the RadicalxChange Foundation, tech-progressive/mechanism-design), Lacey Strahm (VP at OpenMined, privacy-tech nonprofit), and Salomé Viljoen (University of Michigan law professor, data-governance scholar).
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A notable left-right, academic-advocacy coalition around a shared 'data as collective/labor-like right' framework — this kind of unusual coalition is often a precursor to bipartisan legislative movement, worth tracking for early-stage AI/data regulation risk.
insights.locator: Editor’s Note: This policy framework is the product of a 2025-2026 data governance working group

insights.claim: The report explicitly cites Pope Leo XIV's recent encyclical on AI as endorsing the principle of 'subsidiarity' — giving local communities, schools, religious institutions and associations a voice in AI governance decisions — as validation for the DRA model.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Signals explicit Catholic institutional alignment with collective/associational (rather than purely individual or state-centric) AI governance models — relevant to how faith-based advocacy networks may mobilize around AI regulation.
insights.locator: In his recent encyclical on AI, Pope Leo XIV specifically underlined the principle of subsidiarity

insights.claim: The report frames Silicon Valley's AGI race in existential terms, quoting Elon Musk's prediction that AI will be 'unequivocally smarter than humans in every way' within a few years and an unnamed OpenAI employee saying they 'would prefer a world of rapid RSI [recursive self-improvement] and human disempowerment.'
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Uses extreme AGI-acceleration rhetoric from industry insiders to justify urgency for the proposed governance framework — a useful gauge of how AI-safety/disempowerment rhetoric is being mobilized in family-policy advocacy, not just AI-safety circles.
insights.quote: he “would prefer a world of rapid RSI [recursive self-improvement...] and human disempowerment.”
insights.locator: Frontier AI labs (“Big AI”)
